scores.evidence: OT (operational transformation, as in ShareDB): Needs a central server. It's well proven but harder to build correctly yourself.
scores.rationale: Generic claims are accurate (CRDT offline/P2P, OT needs server, Redis pub/sub, one server per doc), but it never reaches hard parts such as rich-text merge, tombstone growth, or durability-before-ack.

scores.evidence: Shortest path to a demo: steps 1, 4, 7, 8, 11 and 15 with Yjs, TipTap and Hocuspocus.
scores.rationale: Covers the main capabilities and is buildable, but leaves undo semantics, scale targets and offline decisions open, and makes suggestion mode optional without justification.

scores.evidence: Run multiple WebSocket servers, using Redis pub/sub so they share updates, with each document handled by one server at a time.
scores.rationale: Recognizable design, but data ownership is unclear, and Phase 1 REST save conflicts with the CRDT update store of Phase 3; 'pub/sub' plus 'one server per doc' is not reconciled.

scores.evidence: Write tests that simulate several users making conflicting edits at once and confirm all copies end up the same. This is the riskiest part of the project, so test it early.
scores.rationale: Convergence testing is early and the server-restart milestone is checkable, but there are no reordering/duplication specifics, no numeric criteria beyond an unjustified 100 ms, and little production validation.

scores.evidence: Set your targets: how many people can edit one document at once, acceptable delay (aim for under 100 ms...
scores.rationale: It defers scale, offline and team decisions to the reader without stating defaults, and gives little sensitivity analysis of what changes if they differ.

scores.evidence: Rate limiting, size limits on documents and updates, and periodic compaction of the stored edit history.
scores.rationale: Failures are listed only as one-line items (crash, drift, XSS, permission bypass) with little detection or recovery, and nothing on duplicates, malicious updates or corruption.

scores.evidence: Monitoring: sync delay, connection counts and alerts if copies of a document drift apart.
scores.rationale: Monitoring is mentioned, but there is nothing on deployment, rollback, migration, ownership or incident response.
There is no cost discussion of infrastructure, storage growth, Redis or build effort.
It recognizes the merge choice is pivotal, but leaves it to the reader and does not address the data format, schema or exit paths; the single-user-first order creates rework risk.

scores.evidence: Suggestion mode (tracked changes), if you need it.
scores.rationale: It mostly uses off-the-shelf libraries and marks some features optional, but it includes a lot of release-phase breadth (DOCX/PDF, mobile) without need, and omits some essentials.

scores.evidence: Milestone: the server restarts while people are editing, and nothing is lost.
scores.rationale: The phases are ordered with milestones and concrete library examples, but the decisions are deferred and the ordering (single-user editor first, auth late) is only partly justified.

checklist.evidence: CRDT (Yjs or Automerge): Recommended. It supports offline editing and peer-to-peer setups, and mature libraries exist.
Choose the document model: plain text, rich text (ProseMirror, TipTap, Lexical, Slate) or block-based.
Write tests that simulate several users making conflicting edits at once and confirm all copies end up the same.
Store CRDT updates on the server, plus periodic snapshots so documents load quickly.
Run multiple WebSocket servers, using Redis pub/sub so they share updates, with each document handled by one server at a time.
Add offline support with a local cache in IndexedDB.
checked on the WebSocket connection as well as the API.
Version history: named snapshots, comparing versions and restoring.
Show who else is in the document: their cursors, selections, names and colors.
Load testing with many simulated editors on one document.

traps.evidence: Phase 1: Single-user editor ... Save and load documents through a simple REST API and database.
the server restarts while people are editing, and nothing is lost.

note: A sensible, library-based outline that builds a single-user editor first and leaves most hard decisions and failure handling unspecified. It has no cost analysis and little operational detail.
